overview: This file contains a wartime Office of War Information inquiry and the State Department’s reply concerning the prewar United States position on the Kwantung Leased Territory. The correspondence reviews the territory’s transfer from Russia to Japan, the 1915 extension of the lease, continuing Chinese sovereignty under the 1898 Russo-Chinese convention, and the effects of Japan’s 1937 administrative changes. The Department emphasizes that dealing with Japan as the territory’s administering authority did not constitute abandonment of China’s sovereign rights and that the United States neither recognized Manchukuo nor accepted the validity of its purported acts.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on the status of the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.from: Robert E. Hull, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: John Herrick, Office of War Information
subfiles.about: The State Department explains the United States’ position on the lease, sovereignty, and administration of the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The reply judges Hancock’s account of the lease substantially correct and directs the Office of War Information to American diplomatic notes and declarations from 1915, 1921–1922, and 1923. It explains that the United States continued to treat Japan as the administering authority without relinquishing the principle that China retained sovereignty under the 1898 Russo-Chinese convention. It also rejects the premise that the territory had been formally incorporated into Manchukuo, describing the 1937 abolition of its governorship and related railway-zone transfers as Japanese administrative measures that did not validate Manchukuo’s authority there.

subfiles.title: Office of War Information request for clarification of Kwantung policy
subfiles.from: Paul M. Hancock, Media Analysis and Language Research Department, Office of War Information
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State, Division of Current Information
subfiles.about: Hancock asks whether the United States recognized the 1915 extension of Japan’s lease and how it regarded the territory’s legal status.
subfiles.summary: Hancock outlines his understanding that Russia transferred the lease to Japan under the Treaty of Portsmouth and that the 1915 agreements extended its term from twenty-five to ninety-nine years. He asks whether the United States recognized that extension and, if not, whether it considered the territory part of Liaoning Province. He also assumes that the territory was incorporated into Manchukuo in 1937, a premise challenged by the State Department’s reply. The letter is dated January 5, 1942, although the reply identifies it as dated January 5, 1943 and the routing notation includes January 20, 1943.

interest: The file offers a concise statement of how the United States separated practical recognition of Japanese administration from recognition of sovereignty, making it useful for studying the legal logic behind American nonrecognition policy. It also records an internal wartime effort to establish an accurate historical line for government information work. The exchange is especially valuable for its discussion of the disputed meaning of Japan’s 1937 administrative reorganization and for the apparent dating inconsistency between Hancock’s letter, its routing notation, and the State Department reply.
